headline: Chips Crack Under Geopolitical Heat as Software Holds the Line
body_html:
Tuesday's mid-session picture is decidedly bifurcated. Of the 550 names in our universe, 311 are trading lower against 236 advancers — a lopsided tape reflecting the weight of surging crude prices and 30-year Treasury yields that have climbed to their highest level since 2007. The catalyst is well-defined: Iran's confirmation that the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed until Washington satisfies interim deal conditions has sent energy markets into a fresh leg higher, dragging bond yields along and pressuring risk appetites across the board.

Sector leadership tells the story starkly. Software is the lone meaningful bright spot, up 1.06% on the session, with Healthcare and Energy posting modest gains of 0.58% and 0.32% respectively. Everything else is in the red. Semiconductors are the session's deepest wound, off 3.85%, with optical and connectivity names bearing the heaviest losses. Fabrinet has plunged 14.58%, the sharpest single-name decline in the universe, while Kulicke & Soffa, FormFactor, Coherent, Credo Technology, and MaxLinear have each shed between 6% and 7% as the chip-supply chain reprices geopolitical risk in real time.

On the upside, N-able leads all gainers with a 4.59% advance, joined by GoDaddy and BlackLine as software names attract defensive rotation. Into the close, watch whether the 30-year yield holds its elevated range and whether oil's continued bid forces another round of sector-rotation selling across industrials and materials, both down more than 1.2% at present.

briefs.headline: Hormuz Closure Keeps Oil Bid Alive, Lifts Energy Sector
briefs.body: Iran signaled Tuesday that the Strait of Hormuz will stay shut pending satisfaction of interim conditions by Washington, keeping crude prices elevated through the morning session. Energy is among the session's few gainers, up 0.32%, as supply-route anxiety offsets broader risk-off selling. The standoff shows no immediate sign of resolution heading into the afternoon.

briefs.headline: 30-Year Yield Reaches Highest Mark in Nearly Two Decades
briefs.body: U.S. 30-year Treasury yields extended their climb Tuesday to levels not seen since 2007, driven by the twin pressures of elevated oil prices and unresolved Middle East tensions. The move is compressing equity multiples broadly, with rate-sensitive sectors including homebuilders — off 1.18% mid-session — absorbing disproportionate selling pressure.

briefs.headline: Fabrinet's Sharp Drop Anchors a Brutal Day for Optical Names
briefs.body: Fabrinet is down 14.58% mid-session, the steepest decline across our 550-name universe, dragging fellow optical and connectivity firms into a cluster of steep losses. Coherent has fallen 6.68% and Credo Technology is off 6.44%, reflecting broad investor concern over supply-chain exposure to geopolitical chokepoints and slowing data-center demand signals.

briefs.headline: China Redirects Oil Tankers as Gulf Chokepoints Grow Risky
briefs.body: Chinese state shipping operators have begun routing tankers outside the Gulf to avoid the Hormuz disruption, according to sourced reports Tuesday. Separately, China returned to oil stockpiling in July, a move that surprised markets and adds another demand variable to an already volatile crude complex. The combination is amplifying uncertainty in global energy supply modeling.

briefs.headline: Brunswick Charts AI-Assisted Course Through Sluggish Boat Market
briefs.body: The parent of Sea Ray is leaning into artificial-intelligence-driven navigation technology and new ancillary revenue streams as a hedge against slowing recreational boat sales. The strategic pivot comes as consumer discretionary names broadly struggle mid-session, with the Consumer sector off 0.15% on the day amid rising yields and geopolitical caution among buyers.

briefs.headline: ABC Parent Files First Amendment Challenge Against Broadcast Regulator
briefs.body: Disney's ABC network initiated legal action against the Federal Communications Commission on Tuesday, arguing the agency's actions violate First Amendment protections. The suit introduces a new regulatory flashpoint for the broadcast industry at a moment when media stocks are already navigating a challenging advertising environment and elevated interest-rate headwinds.
